description: A multidisciplinary team of four from Brazil: Unicamp students/engineers Lucas (Computer Engineering), Marina (Agricultural Engineering), and Rafael (Mechanical Engineering), alongside Bia (Lawyer). Combining software, agriculture, mechanics, and governance, we’re building a playful outpost game in Unity for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.
summary:
Most space games treat living on the Moon like effortless magic, hiding the critical engineering trade-offs that real astronauts face every single day. Artemis X is a strategy game created for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge that puts kids in command of a day-by-day lunar outpost.

Players manage scarce resources—power, water, food, and spare parts—while striving to transform their base from relying on Earth supply deliveries to achieving self-sufficiency. Players dispatch rovers to mine crater water ice and construct vital modules like greenhouses, processing minerals, and electrolyzers. 

The game is powered by real space-weather events from NASA’s DONKI database. When a real solar storm hits, players face authentic engineering dilemmas: retract solar panels and lose power, or keep them deployed and risk hardware damage. Artemis X matters because it turns complex NASA systems engineering and space-weather science into intuitive, hands-on decisions that train the next generation of astronauts.

What It Does & How It Works

Artemis X is a day-by-day lunar base strategy game that trains junior astronauts in resource management, closed-loop life support, and space-weather resilience. Instead of giving players unlimited building resources, the game challenges kids to balance four interconnected resources—Power, Water, Food, and Spare Parts—until their outpost achieves full self-sufficiency and earns up to 3 stars.

The Core Gameplay Loop:

  1. Scout & Harvest: Players dispatch lunar rovers into shadowed craters to extract water ice and regolith while monitoring rover battery levels and mechanical wear.
  2. Build & Process: Players construct real-world lunar habitat modules—including Mineral Processors (for spare parts), Electrolyzers (splitting extracted water into oxygen and fuel), and Greenhouses (turning water and power into sustainable food). Early on, players rely on scheduled Earth Supply Deliveries, gradually weaning off Earth support as their local production scales.
  3. Survive Real NASA Solar Storms: Powered by real space-weather events from NASA’s DONKI database, solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) strike the base. When an alert triggers, players must make an immediate engineering trade-off: retract the solar panels to protect them (causing an immediate power deficit that forces rationing across modules) or leave them deployed to keep life support at 100% while risking severe panel damage that costs scarce spare parts to repair.
  4. Achieve 3-Star Autonomy: Every day survived, module built, and crisis managed scores the player on base efficiency, crew readiness, and self-sufficiency.

Creativity & Design Factors Considered

  • Authentic Trade-Offs Over "Game Over" Screens: When designing for young learners, we wanted failure to teach systems thinking rather than cause frustration. If a player leaves solar panels out during an X-class flare from DONKI, they don't instantly lose—they experience cascading engineering consequences (damaged panels → spare parts shortage → delayed rover maintenance) that mirror real mission planning.
  • Cognitive Load & Accessibility for Kids: Real lunar environmental control (ECLSS) and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) involve complex chemistry and physics. We distilled these systems into clear visual feedback loops, color-coded resource gauges, and named rovers that kids immediately care about protecting.

Intended Impact & Benefits

  • Demystifying Systems Engineering: Kids learn that space exploration isn't just about rockets—it is about sustainability, recycling every drop of water, and making calculated decisions under uncertainty.
  • Space-Weather Literacy: By connecting in-game crises to real NASA DONKI solar events, players discover how the Sun actively shapes human operations on the Moon.
  • Classroom & Museum Ready: Built to run smoothly on web browsers, Artemis X works as a 10-to-15-minute interactive lab for middle-school STEM classrooms, science centers, and self-guided young explorers anywhere in the world.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Game Engine & Logic: Built in Unity using C# with a modular, event-driven architecture separating resource simulation, module state machines, and UI feedback.
  • Platforms: Cross-compiled for WebGL and a future iOS Mobile build, anyone can play without creating an account or downloading the game.
  • Data Integration: Custom NASA DONKI data pipeline translating real solar flare and geomagnetic storm intensity metrics into balanced in-game event probabilities and hazard modifiers.

Custom UI & Original Soundtrack

  • UI/UX Design: Custom kid-friendly HUD, icons layout, and visual feedback loops crafted in Figma.
  • Original Music: Original soundtrack composed from scratch by the team in FL Studio.
